issues.explanation: Pain Recall implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type being trauma to a loved one unless there was also direct physical injury to the patient. That is not otherwise supported by the profile.

Physical Vulnerability and permanent bodily damage imply the patient believes his own body was physically harmed. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this is difficult to explain clinically without evidence that he was also directly injured.

Military Topics is a trigger that suggests a military/combat-linked trauma context, but no other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal item supports a military-related formulation. As a standalone item it feels disconnected from the rest of the profile.

Avoid Driving is plausible for motor-vehicle trauma, but here it lacks support from the trauma type and from the rest of the profile. With no transport-related trigger or memory content, it appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

For trauma to a loved one, visible injuries is a plausible trigger, but darkness and alcohol smell are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Nothing in memory, threat, or appraisals suggests a dark-space or alcohol-related trauma context, so these triggers feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent loved-one trauma presentation.

Avoiding work/study is hard to reconcile with this patient's occupation as a paramedic unless the trauma is clearly tied to the workplace, but the rest of the profile frames the trauma as harm to a loved one rather than occupational trauma. Drug use is also insufficiently supported elsewhere in the profile: there are no other items indicating broad externalising coping or substance-related trigger context, making this strategy feel tacked on.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but this specific wording implies a direct causal role in the event. The rest of the profile does not provide supporting content suggesting he believes his own actions caused the loved one's trauma. The other appraisals are about damage and unreliability of self, so this item is the least integrated with the stated trauma type and surrounding node content.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only trigger that suggests a substance-related context. The other trigger and memory items center on victims/injuries, which fits a paramedic exposed to injured loved ones or victims. Without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content linked to alcohol, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the trauma representation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs
issues.explanation: Drug use can occur in PTSD, but here it is the only maladaptive strategy that implies substance misuse. The rest of the profile emphasizes work avoidance, suppression, sensory reliving, and hypervigilant threat responses. With no parallel alcohol/substance-related trigger, appraisal, or memory content, this item looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, self-blame is plausible only if the patient had a clear perceived role in failing to protect or respond. In this profile, the other items describe reliving of victims/injuries, hypervigilance, and damaged-self beliefs, but nothing else indicates a responsibility-based trauma narrative. This makes the specific self-blame item the least coherent appraisal relative to the rest of the selected content.

vignette: Sami, a 40-year-old Middle Eastern man and paramedic, has been struggling with his mental health ever since he witnessed a traumatic event at work where he failed to save a loved one. The incident occurred during a chaotic scene in a hospital emergency room filled with the antiseptic smell that now triggers intense anxiety for him. He recalls the sight of visible injuries and wounds on others, which only intensify the trauma. Sami’s wife has noticed a significant change in his behavior over the past few months. What frightens her most is when he reacts with alarm to unexpected touches, even from her. His difficulty concentrating at work has led to multiple errors, causing him immense distress. The trauma has left him feeling permanently changed for the worse and questioning his ability to rely on himself. One of Sami’s coping mechanisms involves trying hard not to think about the traumatic event. He suppresses thoughts that come up involuntarily, but this only leads to a cycle where the memories feel completely real when they do surface, reliving all the terror he experienced at the time. This full sensory reliving often happens unpredictably and leaves him feeling helpless and haunted by his failure to protect others. Sami’s constant need to feel safe has made work particularly challenging. He always chooses the safest seat in a vehicle or room, which only highlights how much the trauma has altered his sense of security. The thought that he can’t rely on himself further exacerbates this fear, as he often finds himself hyper-vigilant and startled by even minor events. His efforts to suppress thoughts about the event have led him to overwork at his paramedic job. By throwing himself into tasks, Sami hopes to keep his mind occupied, but this behavior only perpetuates his symptoms. The memories of that day still flood back vividly during moments when he’s overwhelmed by triggers like the antiseptic smell or seeing injured patients. These intense recollections often leave him with memory gaps, where parts of the event remain unclear, adding to his sense of helplessness and guilt. Sami has started avoiding work altogether on days when he feels particularly anxious about encountering these triggers. This avoidance behavior, however, only reinforces his belief that he can’t rely on himself in critical situations, deepening his negative appraisals and making him more vulnerable to further anxiety. His wife’s concern over his deteriorating mental health finally pushed Sami to seek help. What frightens him most is the fear of never recovering from this trauma and becoming permanently damaged. He hopes that with professional support, he can find a way to cope more effectively without feeling like he has failed himself or others again. In therapy sessions, Sami expresses his deepest fears about being forever changed by what happened. These negative appraisals drive much of his behavior and make it challenging for him to feel secure in any environment. His hyper-vigilance and startled reactions only serve to reinforce these beliefs, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that he finds increasingly difficult to break. The memory gaps about the traumatic event further contribute to Sami’s sense of unreliability. He often wonders what parts of the event he has forgotten, which adds to his overall distress and belief in his own failure as a paramedic and protector. These memories, when they do emerge, are so vivid that they feel entirely real, amplifying his fear and reinforcing the cycle of negative appraisals. Sami’s overworking is both a coping mechanism and a manifestation of his guilt. By pushing himself to work harder, he hopes to compensate for what he sees as his failure in protecting others. However, this strategy only leads to more errors at work due to difficulty concentrating, further validating his belief that he can’t rely on himself. Sami’s current state is one of intense anxiety and fear about the future. He has come to believe that he is permanently damaged by what happened and that he will never fully recover. What he most hopes for is a way out of this cycle of trauma and a return to feeling like he can trust himself again.
